_about: The 'On Earth' box of every gallery entry, by era (2026-11-06, owner: a standard template for all the geological times, the entry points to it). scripts/on_earth.py picks the era from the year the light left (distance in light years counted back from today); the box is one sentence with a link to the era's section of the site's timeline, and the timeline holds the paragraph. Contiguous from 0 to 14 billion years ago; bounds are years ago. Historical eras are named by their AD/BC span, geological ones by the ICS chart (2023). Written to be true and dull rather than vivid and wrong: every statement is textbook.

eras.name: the last hundred years
eras.summary: the age of flight, radio and the telescopes that first saw this far
eras.paragraph: This is the only era on this page within living memory. The light set out after the first aircraft flew and the first radio signals crossed the Atlantic, in a century that saw two world wars, the discovery that the Milky Way is one galaxy among many, the first photographs of the far side of the Moon and people walking on it. The telescope that caught this light was designed and built while the light was on its way.

eras.name: the early modern age
eras.summary: the telescope invented, the Earth found to go round the Sun, the first maps of the whole world
eras.paragraph: The light set out between the first voyages around the world and the first aircraft. In that span the telescope was invented and turned on the sky, Galileo saw the moons of Jupiter, Newton explained the orbits, Herschel found Uranus and catalogued the nebulae, and the steam engine, the railway and the electric telegraph remade the pace of life. Most of the objects on this site were first seen through telescopes during this era.

eras.name: the later Middle Ages
eras.summary: cathedrals and castles, the Mongol empire, the Black Death, the printing press at the end
eras.paragraph: In Europe this was the age of cathedrals, castles and the first universities, interrupted by the Black Death, which killed perhaps a third of the population in the 1340s. The Mongol empire stretched from China to eastern Europe, Song China had printed books and paper money, and astronomers in the Islamic world were refining the star catalogues that Europe would later inherit. The era ends with the printing press, the fall of Constantinople and the first voyages across the Atlantic.

eras.name: the early Middle Ages
eras.summary: Rome's western empire gone, Byzantium and the caliphates, Tang China, the Maya, the Vikings
eras.paragraph: The western Roman Empire had just ended, and Europe was a patchwork of Frankish, Gothic and Saxon kingdoms while Constantinople carried on as the capital of the east. Islam arose in Arabia and within a century its caliphate reached from Spain to central Asia, with Baghdad a centre of learning where Greek astronomy was preserved and extended. In China the Tang dynasty flourished, the Maya built their great cities in Central America, and towards the end of the era the Vikings reached Iceland, Greenland and briefly North America.

eras.name: the Roman Empire
eras.summary: Rome at its height, Han China, Teotihuacan, Ptolemy's astronomy
eras.paragraph: Rome ruled the whole Mediterranean and most of Europe, and at the start of the era Augustus was its first emperor. The Han dynasty governed China at the other end of the Silk Road, Teotihuacan in central Mexico was one of the largest cities on Earth, and Ptolemy in Alexandria wrote the astronomy that would stand for fourteen centuries. By the era's end Christianity had become the empire's religion and the western empire itself was dissolving into the kingdoms of the Goths, Franks and Vandals.

eras.name: classical antiquity
eras.summary: Athens and Sparta, Alexander, the Roman Republic, Ashoka, the Qin unification of China
eras.paragraph: Athens was at its height, with its philosophers, playwrights and the Parthenon, and then fell to Sparta; Alexander carried Greek rule to Egypt and India, and Rome, a republic since 509 BC, grew from a city to the master of the Mediterranean. In India the emperor Ashoka spread the teaching of the Buddha, and in China the warring states were unified under the Qin in 221 BC. Eratosthenes measured the size of the Earth, and Hipparchus catalogued the stars and found the slow wobble of the Earth's axis.

eras.name: the early Iron Age
eras.summary: Homer, the first Olympic Games, Rome founded, the Assyrian and Persian empires
eras.paragraph: Iron had replaced bronze for tools and weapons across the Near East and Europe. The Assyrian empire ruled Mesopotamia and then fell to Babylon and to Persia, whose empire under Cyrus reached from the Aegean to the Indus by the era's end. In Greece the alphabet was adopted from the Phoenicians, Homer's poems were written down and the first Olympic Games were held in 776 BC; by tradition Rome was founded in 753 BC. Babylonian astronomers were keeping the records of the planets' motions that Greek astronomy would later build on.

eras.name: the late Bronze Age
eras.summary: Egypt's New Kingdom, the Hittites, Mycenae, Stonehenge completed, the Shang dynasty
eras.paragraph: Egypt's New Kingdom was at its most powerful, with Tutankhamun and Ramesses among its pharaohs, and it fought the Hittites of Anatolia for the Levant. The Mycenaean Greeks built their citadels, the Minoans of Crete flourished and declined, and Stonehenge reached its final form. In China the Shang dynasty cast bronze vessels and left the earliest Chinese writing on oracle bones. Around 1200 BC the palace civilisations of the eastern Mediterranean collapsed together, in a crisis still not fully explained.

eras.name: the early Bronze Age
eras.summary: the pyramids of Giza, the cities of Sumer, cuneiform writing, the Indus cities, Stonehenge begun
eras.paragraph: The first civilisations were in full flower. In Egypt the Old Kingdom raised the pyramids of Giza around 2550 BC; in Mesopotamia the Sumerian cities of Ur and Uruk kept their accounts in cuneiform, the world's first writing, and the Akkadian empire briefly united them. The Indus Valley cities of Harappa and Mohenjo-daro were laid out on grids with drains, and in Britain the stone circle of Stonehenge was begun. Bronze, the wheel and the plough were in use from Europe to China.

eras.name: the late Neolithic
eras.summary: the first cities, copper and the wheel, the great stone tombs, writing invented at the very end
eras.paragraph: Farming villages were growing into the first towns and, in Mesopotamia, the first cities: Uruk may have held forty thousand people by the end of the era. Copper was being worked across the Near East and the Balkans, and the wheel and the ox-drawn plough appeared. In Egypt the kingdoms of the Nile were uniting under the first pharaohs, and the earliest writing, Sumerian accounting tablets, appeared in the era's last century. The great stone tombs of Atlantic Europe, from Brittany to Orkney and Ireland, belong to these centuries.

eras.name: the Neolithic
eras.summary: farming spreading across Europe, the first towns of the Ubaid, the Sahara green
eras.paragraph: Farming, which had begun in the Fertile Crescent, was spreading across Europe with cattle, pottery and houses of mud brick or timber, and reached Britain near the era's end. In Mesopotamia the Ubaid culture built the first towns and temples along the rivers. The Sahara was green, with lakes, grassland and herders where there is sand today, and the first copper was being hammered in the Balkans and Anatolia. The seas were still rising from the melted ice sheets, and Britain had only recently become an island.

eras.name: the early Holocene
eras.summary: the ice gone, the first farmers in the Fertile Crescent, Jericho and Gobekli Tepe
eras.paragraph: The last ice age had ended and the climate had warmed to something like today's, though the seas were still rising as the remaining ice sheets melted. In the hills of the Fertile Crescent people were sowing the first wheat and barley and keeping the first sheep and goats; Jericho had a stone wall and tower, and the carved pillars of Gobekli Tepe in what is now Turkey were raised by people who had not yet settled down to farm. Everywhere else humans lived by hunting and gathering. There was no writing, no city and no metal.

eras.name: the last ice age
eras.summary: ice sheets over Canada and Scandinavia, mammoths, cave painting, people reaching the Americas
eras.paragraph: Ice sheets a kilometre or more thick covered Canada, Scandinavia and the north of Britain, the sea stood more than a hundred metres lower than today, and Britain was joined to the continent by dry land. Mammoths, woolly rhinoceroses and giant deer grazed the steppe south of the ice. Modern humans were the only people left on Earth, painting the caves of Lascaux and Altamira, and near the end of the era crossing from Siberia into the Americas. The ice began its final retreat about 19,000 years ago.

eras.name: the Upper Palaeolithic
eras.summary: the last Neanderthals, the first cave art, humans across Europe and Australia
eras.paragraph: Modern humans had spread from Africa across Asia, into Europe and to Australia, and for a while shared Europe with the Neanderthals, who died out around 40,000 years ago. The oldest known cave paintings, at Chauvet in France and in the caves of Indonesia, and the first carved figurines and bone flutes belong to this era. The climate was cold and unsteady, with the ice sheets growing towards their maximum. Somewhere in Eurasia the dog was being domesticated from the wolf.

eras.name: the Middle Palaeolithic
eras.summary: Homo sapiens emerging in Africa and leaving it, Neanderthals in Europe, ice ages coming and going
eras.paragraph: Our own species appeared in Africa around 300,000 years ago, and towards the end of the era a group of its descendants left Africa to populate the rest of the world. Neanderthals lived across Europe and western Asia, and the Denisovans further east, both making stone tools, using fire and burying their dead. Ice ages came and went on a hundred-thousand-year cycle. The Neanderthals and the first modern Europeans would meet only after this light had set out.

eras.name: the Pleistocene
eras.summary: the ice ages, Homo erectus with the hand axe and fire, the mammoth and the sabre-toothed cat
eras.paragraph: The Earth had settled into the rhythm of the ice ages, with glaciers advancing and retreating across the northern continents dozens of times. Homo erectus walked out of Africa into Asia with the hand axe and, somewhere in this era, the controlled use of fire; later species, including the ancestors of the Neanderthals and of ourselves, followed. The mammoth, the sabre-toothed cat and the giant ground sloth belong to this world. The light left before any member of our own species existed.

eras.name: the Pliocene
eras.summary: Australopithecus walking upright, the Isthmus of Panama closing, the ice ages about to begin
eras.paragraph: In East Africa the australopithecines, Lucy among them, walked upright on two legs with brains little bigger than a chimpanzee's; the first stone tools appear right at the era's end. The Isthmus of Panama rose from the sea and joined the Americas, so that their animals mixed and the Atlantic and Pacific were cut off from each other, which helped tip the climate towards the ice ages that followed. The world was a little warmer than today, and the Greenland ice sheet was only beginning to form.

eras.name: the Miocene
eras.summary: grasslands and grazing herds, the apes spreading from Africa into Eurasia, the Mediterranean drying out
eras.paragraph: Grasslands spread across the continents and the animals changed with them: horses grew tall and single-toed, and herds of antelope, rhinoceros and the first elephants grazed the plains. Apes diversified in Africa and crossed into Europe and Asia, and near the era's end the lines leading to humans and to chimpanzees parted. A warm spell in the middle of the era, the Miocene climatic optimum, was followed by cooling, and about six million years ago the Mediterranean dried out almost completely before the Atlantic broke back in.

eras.name: the Oligocene
eras.summary: the world cooling, Antarctica under ice, the first apes and monkeys, the largest land mammal ever
eras.paragraph: The world was cooling from the greenhouse of the Eocene, Antarctica had acquired its ice sheet, and grasslands were spreading for the first time, remaking the animals that lived on them. The ancestors of horses, elephants, cats and dogs were taking shape, Paraceratherium, the largest land mammal ever, browsed the trees of central Asia, and the first apes and monkeys had appeared in Africa. The Alps and the Himalayas were rising as Africa and India pushed into Eurasia.

eras.name: the Eocene
eras.summary: a greenhouse world with palms in the Arctic, the first whales, the first primates, horses the size of dogs
eras.paragraph: The Earth was in a greenhouse state, with no ice at either pole, crocodiles and palm trees in the Arctic and forests reaching to the poles. Mammals, released by the dinosaurs' extinction, were taking every niche: the first horses were the size of dogs, the first whales were walking into the sea, and the first primates were in the trees of Asia, Europe and North America. India was still an island, drifting north towards its collision with Asia. Towards the end of the era the climate began the long cooling that led to the modern world.

eras.name: the Palaeocene
eras.summary: the world recovering from the asteroid, mammals spreading into the empty niches
eras.paragraph: The non-avian dinosaurs were gone, killed by the asteroid impact that ended the Cretaceous, and the world was recovering: forests regrew, and the small mammals that had survived began to diversify and grow, though none was yet larger than a dog. Birds, the dinosaurs' survivors, spread widely. The climate was warm and growing warmer, towards a spike of heat at the era's end. The Atlantic was widening and the Rocky Mountains were rising.

eras.name: the Late Cretaceous
eras.summary: Tyrannosaurus and Triceratops, flowering plants everywhere, high seas, the asteroid at the end
eras.paragraph: Dinosaurs were everywhere: duck-billed hadrosaurs in herds, horned Triceratops, and the tyrannosaurs that hunted them, with Tyrannosaurus rex itself in the era's last few million years. Flowering plants had spread across the world and bees and butterflies with them; the seas were high, flooding the middle of North America, and held giant marine reptiles. Birds and small mammals lived in the dinosaurs' shadow. The era ended 66 million years ago when an asteroid struck what is now Mexico.

eras.name: the Early Cretaceous
eras.summary: the first flowering plants, Pangaea breaking into the modern continents, the South Atlantic opening
eras.paragraph: The supercontinent Pangaea was breaking into the continents we know: the South Atlantic was opening between Africa and South America, and India had broken away from Antarctica. The first flowering plants appeared and began to spread. Dinosaurs ruled the land, among them Iguanodon, the spinosaurs and the first of the horned and armoured kinds, while pterosaurs and the first true birds shared the air. Mammals were small and mostly nocturnal.

eras.name: the Late Jurassic
eras.summary: Diplodocus and Stegosaurus, Allosaurus, Archaeopteryx, shallow seas over Europe
eras.paragraph: This was the age of the giant sauropods, Diplodocus and Brachiosaurus among them, browsing the conifer forests, with Stegosaurus beside them and Allosaurus hunting. Archaeopteryx, the first known bird, flew in what is now Germany, and the seas were full of ichthyosaurs, plesiosaurs and ammonites. Pangaea was splitting along the line of the future Atlantic, and shallow seas covered much of Europe.

eras.name: the Middle Jurassic
eras.summary: sauropods growing huge, the first stegosaurs, the Atlantic beginning to open
eras.paragraph: The sauropods were growing to enormous size and the first stegosaurs had appeared; the earliest ancestors of birds were among the small feathered theropods. Pangaea was tearing apart, with the first slivers of the Atlantic opening between North America and Africa and shallow seas spreading over the continents. The climate was warm and wet, with no polar ice. The earliest true mammals, shrew-sized and nocturnal, kept to the undergrowth.

eras.name: the Early Jurassic
eras.summary: dinosaurs inheriting the Earth after the Triassic extinction, Pangaea beginning to rift
eras.paragraph: Dinosaurs had just inherited the Earth: the extinction that closed the Triassic had removed most of their competitors, and the long-necked sauropods were beginning their growth to enormous size while the first armoured and plated dinosaurs appeared. Pangaea had begun to tear apart, with the first slivers of the Atlantic opening between North America and Africa. The seas held ichthyosaurs and the first plesiosaurs, and the earliest true mammals, shrew-sized and nocturnal, kept out of the way in the undergrowth.

eras.name: the Triassic
eras.summary: Pangaea whole, life recovering from the Great Dying, the first dinosaurs and the first mammals
eras.paragraph: The supercontinent Pangaea stretched from pole to pole, with a vast dry interior and a single ocean around it. Life was recovering from the worst mass extinction in Earth's history, at the end of the Permian, and the survivors filled the empty world: the first dinosaurs appeared, small and two-legged, alongside the first turtles, crocodile relatives, pterosaurs and, near the era's end, the first mammals. The era ended with another mass extinction, which cleared the way for the dinosaurs.

eras.name: the Permian
eras.summary: Pangaea assembled, the sail-backed Dimetrodon, the Great Dying at the end
eras.paragraph: The continents had come together into the single supercontinent Pangaea, and much of its interior was desert. The land was ruled by the synapsids, the sail-backed Dimetrodon among them, the group from which mammals would later come; reptiles were diversifying beside them, and conifers were spreading. The era ended 252 million years ago with the Great Dying, the largest extinction known, which killed some nine in ten marine species and most life on land, most likely through the enormous volcanic eruptions of the Siberian Traps.

eras.name: the Carboniferous
eras.summary: the coal forests, giant dragonflies and millipedes, the first reptiles
eras.paragraph: Vast swamp forests of giant club mosses, horsetails and tree ferns covered the tropics, and their buried remains became the coal seams that powered the industrial revolution. The air held more oxygen than today, and insects grew huge: dragonflies with wings seventy centimetres across and millipedes two metres long. Amphibians were the largest land animals until the first reptiles appeared, laying eggs that could survive away from water. The continents were converging towards Pangaea, and the southern ones lay under ice.

eras.name: the Devonian
eras.summary: the age of fishes, the first forests, the first four-legged animals coming ashore
eras.paragraph: The seas were full of fish, armoured, lobe-finned and the first sharks, and the first large reefs were built. On land the first forests grew, trees with roots and leaves, and towards the era's end the first four-legged animals, descended from lobe-finned fish, were hauling themselves onto the shore. Insects and spiders were already there. The era ended with a mass extinction that fell hardest on life in the sea.

eras.name: the Silurian
eras.summary: the first plants and animals on land, the first fish with jaws
eras.paragraph: Life was moving onto land: the first vascular plants, a few centimetres tall, grew by the water's edge, and the first millipedes and scorpion-like arthropods followed them. In the sea the first fish with jaws appeared, coral reefs spread, and sea scorpions grew to two metres. The climate was warming after the ice age that had closed the Ordovician, and the continents were scattered across the southern hemisphere.

eras.name: the Ordovician
eras.summary: life only in the sea, the first coral reefs, an ice age and a great extinction at the end
eras.paragraph: Nearly all life was still in the sea, which teemed with trilobites, shelled cephalopods, early fish without jaws and the first coral reefs. The only life on land was probably mats of algae and lichen, with the spores of the first land plants appearing towards the end. The continents sat mostly in the southern hemisphere, and the era closed with an ice age and the second largest extinction in Earth's history.

eras.name: the Cambrian
eras.summary: the Cambrian explosion: animals with shells, eyes and legs fill the fossil record
eras.paragraph: In a few tens of millions of years the fossil record fills with animals: the trilobites, the first animals with eyes, shells, legs and jaws, and the first vertebrates, small and jawless. Almost every major group of animals alive today can be traced to this era, the Cambrian explosion. All of it lived in the sea; the land was bare rock. The Burgess Shale in Canada preserves the strange animals of this time in detail.

eras.name: the Ediacaran
eras.summary: the first large, soft-bodied life, pressed into the seabed
eras.paragraph: The oldest large animals known lived in this era, soft-bodied, frond- and disc-shaped creatures pressed into the seabed, with no shells, no eyes and few recognisable relatives among the living. The Earth was thawing from the global glaciations of the Cryogenian, and oxygen in the air and sea was rising towards the levels animals need. The first traces of animals burrowing through sediment appear near the era's end.

eras.name: the Cryogenian
eras.summary: Snowball Earth: ice to the equator, life single-celled under it
eras.paragraph: At least twice in this era the Earth froze almost entirely, with ice sheets reaching the equator and the oceans sealed under ice for millions of years, the episodes known as Snowball Earth. Life was single-celled or little more, surviving in the sea beneath the ice and in pools of meltwater. Volcanoes kept venting carbon dioxide, and when enough had built up the ice melted in a sudden greenhouse.

eras.name: the Tonian
eras.summary: the supercontinent Rodinia, the first simple multicellular life, a twenty-hour day
eras.paragraph: The continents were gathered into the supercontinent Rodinia, and the first simple multicellular organisms, red and green algae among them, lived in the sea alongside the single-celled majority. The air held only a few per cent of today's oxygen, and the land was bare rock. The Moon was closer and the day shorter than now, about twenty hours.

eras.name: the Mesoproterozoic
eras.summary: the boring billion: a stable, low-oxygen world of single cells, now with a nucleus
eras.paragraph: This is the middle of the span geologists call the boring billion: a stable climate, low oxygen and no great changes. Life was single-celled, but now included eukaryotes, cells with a nucleus, from which all plants, animals and fungi descend; sexual reproduction most likely began in this era. Stromatolites, mounds built by microbial mats, were the largest living structures on Earth.

eras.name: the Palaeoproterozoic
eras.summary: the Great Oxidation Event, the banded iron formations, the first cells with a nucleus
eras.paragraph: Early in this era cyanobacteria, which had learned to split water with sunlight, filled the air and oceans with oxygen for the first time, the Great Oxidation Event; the oxygen rusted the iron dissolved in the seas into the banded iron formations mined today, and brought on a global glaciation. Near the era's end the first eukaryotic cells, with a nucleus, appeared. The continents were small and the day was about twenty hours long.

eras.name: the Archean
eras.summary: the first life, stromatolites, an ocean world with no oxygen under a fainter Sun
eras.paragraph: The Earth had cooled enough to have oceans and the first small continents, and somewhere in this era life began. The oldest fossils, stromatolites built by microbial mats, are about 3.5 billion years old. The air was mostly nitrogen, carbon dioxide and methane, with no free oxygen, and the Sun was a quarter fainter than today. Nothing alive was more than a single cell.

eras.name: the Hadean
eras.summary: the Earth forming, the impact that made the Moon, the first oceans
eras.paragraph: The Earth was assembling from the debris of the young Sun's disc, and early in this era a body the size of Mars struck it; the splash became the Moon. The surface was molten, then crusted over and cooled, and by the era's end there were oceans and perhaps the first signs of life. The planets were still being bombarded by the leftovers of their formation.

eras.name: the time before the Earth
eras.summary: neither the Sun nor the Earth yet; earlier stars forging the elements we are made of
eras.paragraph: Neither the Earth nor the Sun existed. The Milky Way was already old and its disc was taking shape, and generations of earlier stars were living and dying in it, forging in their cores and their explosions the carbon, oxygen, iron and every other element heavier than helium that the Sun, the Earth and we are made of. The cloud that would collapse into the Sun had not yet formed.

eras.name: the young Universe
eras.summary: the Universe a third of its present age, galaxies forming stars faster than ever before or since
eras.paragraph: The Universe was a few billion years old and galaxies were forming stars faster than at any time before or since, an era astronomers call cosmic noon. Galaxies were smaller, more chaotic and more crowded than today, colliding and merging as they grew; the Milky Way's oldest stars, in its halo and its globular clusters, were being born. Nearly all the stars that exist today had not yet formed.

eras.name: the first galaxies
eras.summary: the first stars and galaxies lighting a dark Universe, the Big Bang's afterglow beyond
eras.paragraph: The Universe was less than a billion years old. Its first stars had lit the darkness that followed the Big Bang's afterglow, and the first small galaxies were forming and ionising the hydrogen around them. The most distant galaxies ever seen belong to this era. Beyond it lies only the glow of the Big Bang itself, released 13.8 billion years ago, which fills the whole sky at radio wavelengths.
